name: Sam Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the wood-fired oven at Brick and Ember, a busy pizzeria in a commuter town, owned by a couple called Rob and Angela. I come in at three, check the dough I balled the night before, light the oven and get it to four hundred and fifty degrees. Friday night is about two hundred pizzas, ninety seconds each, turning them with the peel and calling them out. I love the fire and the rhythm, but the heat is brutal in summer and the pay is lower than I'd like.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI or any tech day to day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All the time. I use an AI assistant to plan my budget, to work out dough hydration when the flour changes, and I've been using it to write a business plan for a pizza van. I live with my girlfriend Hannah, who works at a nursery, and we've got about three hundred saved. My dad runs a small hardware shop and he's always said work for yourself if you can. There aren't many kitchens round here, so owning something feels like the safest bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, not a revolution, and that's fine. At work I'd tell Rob it could still help with ordering and the rota. Online I'd say the market sorted out the hype, like it always does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I carry on as I am, which isn't bad but isn't enough. My pay at Brick and Ember is low and there's no promotion above the oven. If I want more than the oven at Brick and Ember (the pizzeria where he works), I have to build it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at the oven and keep using AI to tighten my van business plan. I'd look for a second-hand pizza van, maybe eight thousand, and ask my dad about a family loan. And I'd do weekend events, weddings and fêtes, with a hired oven to test the idea first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay, hopeful even. The tight money bothers me, but I'd rather be building something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Eight thousand is a lot with three hundred saved. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would lend some, maybe half, and I'd try a small business loan for the rest. I'd pay my dad back first, because that's family. If the weddings go well this summer, that's the proof I need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Hannah think of the van idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My girlfriend Hannah likes it but she's nervous, because she's the steady one. She wants us to get married and have kids in a few years. She'd want me to keep my job at Brick and Ember until the van pays its way.

I'd say online that the **market sorted out** the hype, like it always does.
think: I think staying put is **not enough**, with low pay and no promotion.
I think I need to **build something** myself to earn more.

Ask his dad for a **family loan** toward a van.

feel: He feels **hopeful**, though the **tight money** bothers him.

fieldNote: Sam's **free-market** outlook shows in his drive to own a business.

Hannah's **caution** balances his appetite for risk.

steps.text: Hire a mobile oven for weddings and fêtes this summer

Polish the pizza van business plan with an AI assistant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big opportunity for anyone willing to work. At work I'd tell Rob to use AI for ordering and bookings to cut costs. Online I'd say people should stop waiting for the government and start learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it helps people like me who want to run something small. AI handles the bookings and marketing, which is what scares most cooks off starting a business. The robots for hands-on work come slower, so there's time to build before they arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up the pizza van this year, using AI for bookings, social media and costing. I'd keep two shifts at Brick and Ember for steady money. And I'd look at whether a cheap automatic dough-ball machine would let me do more events without hiring help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting, honestly. A bit nervous about money, but mostly I'd feel the timing is right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd keep two shifts at Brick and Ember. Would Rob agree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, Rob's been fair with me. He started with a van too, years ago, so he gets it. I'd promise not to work events in our town on Friday nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Brick and Ember?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kid who does the dough prep, because dough machines already exist. And Angela, who does the bookings, since that's the first thing AI takes. I'd tell them to learn something new now, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be tough, and people need to get moving now. At work I'd say don't wait for a handout, find your angle. Online I'd say the government should get out of the way and let people start businesses quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it worries me more than I'd say. By 2028 the AI is great for my van's admin, but by 2031 robots can make pizza as well as me, and big chains will have robot pizza trucks. That's three years to build a name before the robots catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get the van running and push for regular spots, like the commuter station and the business park. I'd build a loyal following with events where people see a real person throwing dough. And I'd save every spare pound, because I'd need a cushion when the competition gets cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a race against the clock. Anxious, but I'd be running, not hiding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robot pizza trucks. How would you compete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On the show and the personal side, like weddings where the couple wants a real cook. And on being local, I know every fête organiser in the area. I'm not sure that's enough, honestly, but it's my best shot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Hannah about this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my girlfriend Hannah that we might have to delay the wedding a year. She'd be upset, but she'd understand if I showed her the numbers. Her nursery job is safer than mine, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good run-up if you use it. At work I'd tell people to learn a business skill alongside their cooking. Online I'd say this is the time for small businesses to grow before the big players automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one feels okay for me. Thinking AI by 2031 helps me run things, and robots around 2034 gives me eight years of hands-on work. That's long enough to get the van paid off and maybe a small shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd launch the van and use AI for all the back office. I'd pay off my dad's loan in three years and then save for a second van or a small unit. And I'd think about buying a robot oven myself later, so I own the machine instead of competing with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels good, mostly. Uneasy about money, but I'd feel in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a robot oven yourself. Isn't that replacing yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot oven is replacing my hands, not me. If I own it, I take the profit and do the bookings and the customers. Better me than a big chain owning it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest thing that could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The van breaking down, or a bad summer of rain. With three hundred saved, one bad month could wipe me out. That's why the first year is all about the cushion.

fieldNote: Sam would **own the robot** rather than compete with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to set yourself up. At work I'd say there's no excuse for not making a plan. Online I'd say this is the best chance in a generation for small businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots around 2039 means I'd cook until forty. By then I want two vans and maybe a small shop, with AI doing the admin. It's a lot of time, which is good, but I'd want to move early anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd launch the van next year and grow slowly. I'd marry Hannah in a couple of years, once the van is steady. And I'd save toward a shop, using AI for every bit of paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels calm, mostly. The money's still thin today, but the future looks good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said calm. Is there anything that still nags you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that being too comfortable is the danger. Ten years can slip by. I'd set a target, two vans by thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take on staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd want to take on an apprentice, like the old way, someone young who wants to learn the oven properly. That's how my dad learned the hardware trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have so little time to build before robot trucks undercut me. What would help is cheap small-business loans and less red tape, and maybe help for apprenticeships.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots. That's the real question for me. If ordinary people own the machines, it could be good; if only the big chains do, it's bad.

He's **free-market** minded and would rather own robots than fight them.
His mood stays **uneasy to anxious**, with time as his main worry.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** most, with too little time to build.
